_schema.note: Every item is a measured perception paired with a measured reality. Nothing here is modelled or estimated by us.

fields.ask: the question as posed to the reader
fields.unit: what the number counts, for the sprite caption
fields.verified: true = I read the number off the primary source in this session
fields.note: anything the caption must say to stay honest
fields.gap: DERIVED: perceived - actual. null where meaningless (trend rows, where actual is a flag not a value)
fields.ratio: DERIVED: perceived / actual, rounded to 1dp. null for trend rows and anywhere actual is 0

_schema.sprite_hint: perceived and actual are percentages, so 'out of every 100' renders directly as sprite counts. Round for display; keep the decimal here.
_schema.quiz_note: QUIZ ITEMS INVERT THE USUAL FIELDS. There is no average estimate published for these, only the share who picked the right option from three. So: perceived = % who answered CORRECTLY, actual = 33.3, the score random guessing would produce. A quiz item is damning when perceived < actual, which is the opposite reading from every other kind here. Any renderer must special-case them.
_schema.derived_note: gap and ratio are computed from perceived/actual by export_perception_xlsx.py and written back here so the JSON and the spreadsheet never disagree. Never hand-edit them. For quiz rows gap is negative when people do worse than chance, which is the damning direction.
_schema.findings_note: Claims about what MAKES the gap wider. These are multipliers and directions, not perceived/actual pairs, so they are not items and cannot be rendered as sprite cards. They are the mechanism behind the numbers - cite them in writing.

items.ask: Out of every 100 Americans, how many think there is more crime in the U.S. than a year ago?
items.note: 64% said crime rose. FBI data showed US crime FELL 4.5% in 2024. The 64% is reported as the prior-year figure in Gallup's 2025 release; actual=0 marks 'crime did not rise', matching the homicide-vs-2000 convention.

items.ask: Out of every 100 Americans, how many think there is more crime in the U.S. than a year ago?
items.note: Down 15 points from 2024 - the gap narrowed but did not close. Weaker instance than the 2024 item; useful mainly as the pair showing perception tracking reality late.

items.ask: Out of every 100 Americans, how many think there is more crime in their own local area than a year ago?
items.note: Pairs with crime-up-us-2025: 49% say the nation got worse, only 30% say their own area did. The gap between the two IS the story - people trust what they see locally and distrust the picture they are given of everywhere else.

items.ask: Out of every 100 people in rich countries, how many know that 60% of girls in low-income countries finish primary school?
items.note: Options were 20% / 40% / 60%; correct is 60%. Only 7% picked it - random guessing scores 33%. The ONLY question in the study whose per-question rate is published online; the rest are in the book's appendix (p.267).

items.ask: Out of every 100 fact questions, how many does the average person in a rich country get right?
items.note: Average score 2.2 of 12 = 18.3%. Random guessing on three options scores 4 of 12 = 33.3%. People perform WORSE than chance, which requires systematically wrong beliefs - ignorance alone would score 33%. Also: 15% got all twelve wrong; only 10% beat random.

items.ask: Out of every 100 people in rich countries, how many know climate experts expect warming over the next 100 years?
items.note: THE CONTROL CASE. 87% correct - so far above chance that Gapminder dropped it from the scored set. Proves the other results are not general stupidity or bad question design: where the message has been transmitted loudly and repeatedly, people know it.

items.ask: Out of every 100 people living in Italy, how many are immigrants?
items.note: Only the US, Italy and Sweden figures appear as numbers in the paper's text; the UK, France and Germany values are in Figure 2 only and are NOT transcribed here. n is the six-country total, roughly 4,000 per country.

items.note: Only the US, Italy and Sweden figures appear as numbers in the paper's text; the UK, France and Germany values are in Figure 2 only and are NOT transcribed here. n is the six-country total, roughly 4,000 per country. items.ask: Out of every 100 Americans, how many are gay or lesbian?
items.note: Gallup's own comparison in this release: an average estimate of ~23.6% against its 4.5% LGBT self-identification figure (2017). Note the benchmark is LGBT overall, which is BROADER than the question asked. Gallup's 2023 breakdown puts gay and lesbian at 'slightly over 1%' each of US adults - roughly 2.5% combined - so the like-for-like gap is larger still, closer to 9x than 5x. Cite 4.5% as 'LGBT', never as 'gay or lesbian'.

Note the benchmark is LGBT overall, which is BROADER than the question asked. Gallup's 2023 breakdown puts gay and lesbian at 'slightly over 1%' each of US adults - roughly 2.5% combined - so the like-for-like gap is larger still, closer to 9x than 5x. items.ask: Out of every 100 people living in the United States, how many are immigrants?
items.note: Pairs with immigrants-us (Ipsos 2024: 30 perceived vs 15 actual). The two DISAGREE on the actual share because they count different things - Alesina uses legal immigrants (10%), Ipsos uses foreign-born (15%) - and the waves are six years apart. Never present them as the same measurement; either is fine alone, with its year.

queued.note: Real leads, numbers NOT yet verified. Do not publish any of these until the primary source is read.
mines: Gapminder / Factfulness 13-question test. Overall results verified: 2017, 14 countries, 10,000+ respondents, average 2.2 correct of 12 against 4 for random guessing, 15% scored zero. PER-QUESTION percentages are only in the book's appendix (p.267) - not on the website. Someone needs the book.

Ipsos Perils of Perception earlier waves, each a separate deck: 2014 (14 countries), 2015 (33), 2016 (40, incl. homophobia and anti-abortion sentiment), 2017 (38), 2020 (32, causes of death), 2021 (30, environment), 2023 (10, conspiracy belief). The 2020 causes-of-death wave and the 2016 wave are the richest untapped ones.

Our World in Data, 'Does the news reflect what we die from?' - heart disease and cancer are 56% of deaths among 15 causes but 7% of coverage; homicide gets 43x its share, terrorism over 18,000x. Not a guess-vs-reality item as it stands, but pairs perfectly with a 'what kills people' question.
Gallup crime series - ~80% thought crime rose in 2023 when it fell; violent victimisation went 80 per 1,000 (1994) to 19 per 1,000 (2010).
Bobby Duffy, 'The Perils of Perception' (2018) - book-length index of the Ipsos waves.
Ahler & Sood MTurk replications in the same paper (n = 382 / 1,036 / 821) - per-party breakdowns of the same eight items.
PNAS Nexus 2024 ingroup-norm work - people overestimate how much their OWN side dislikes the other. The 'undercounting your own side' direction, and nobody has built it.

findings.claim: People who consume news "most of the time" are almost three times as inaccurate as those who consume it "only now and then".
findings.why: Directly inverts the assumption that more news means a better-informed picture of the other side. More exposure, worse model.

findings.claim: Those who post about politics on social media show a substantially larger Perception Gap than those who do not.
findings.why: Participation, not just consumption, tracks with distortion.

findings.claim: Consumption of most forms of media - talk radio, newspapers, social media and local news - is associated with a wider Perception Gap.
findings.why: Not a cable-news or partisan-media effect. Newspapers and local news are on the list too. Do not let this be read as a claim about one outlet.

findings.claim: Higher education among Democrats, but not Republicans, corresponds with a wider Perception Gap. Democrats with a postgraduate degree are three times as inaccurate as those who did not graduate high school.
findings.why: Education does not fix it and for one side makes it worse. The report attributes this partly to friendship diversity: higher-educated Democrats are likelier to say almost all their friends share their politics.

findings.claim: The wider a person's Perception Gap, the more likely they are to attribute negative personal qualities - "hateful", "brainwashed" - to their opponents.
findings.why: The link from misperception to contempt. This is why the gap matters rather than being a trivia result.
